segments.description: Please welcome Shane Tab and Jay Deacon to the Virtual Grand Samp Coaches Conference. Shane is an accomplished tennis coach and educator with multiple accolades, including the Gold Coast Coach Recognition Award in 2018, the Club Recognition Award in 2019, and the Queensland Coaching Excellence Development Award in 2021 and 2024. He is also a Newcombe Coach Excellence finalist for development in 2024. Shane has coached two-time National Champion Tori Russell, developed ITF Junior and National Level Athletes, and mentored multiple NDS and Super 10 level players. Shane co-created the Colourball Circuit for the Gold Coast, established the Bolt Brisbane Finals, and is a valued member of the Tennis Australia Coach Coalition Development Team and TQ Competitive Play Committee presenting workshops nationwide. Jay is a highly accomplished coach, educator, and former elite athlete with expertise across multiple sports. In tennis, he has coached six national age champions to number one, developed innovative programs like Tennis Hot Shots Talent Camps, and the Red, Orange and Green Tournament Circuits and led 12 consecutive Premiership Teams. A former number one ranked Australian swimmer and international water polo competitor, Jay has also coached national champions and future Olympians. As a Tennis Australia Coach Developer, University Electro and ABC Radio Commentator, Jay combines his passion for sport with education and innovation.

Together, they share invaluable insights into creating Colourball Leagues. Welcome Jay and Shane. The premise behind it was that we came across some interesting data that was collected that if a child hasn't played, had a competitive experience in their first year of play, and this is going from four to 12, there's an 80% chance that they're going to drop out of the sport. So we considered that and we knew that this was the case going into our discussions about how we improve things on the Gold Coast. We started with the theory that in-house or intra-club match play was a big part of something that we could offer as an outcome, rather than just having a lesson each week. So the idea then was that they would have lessons, play match play within the club, and then from there we built out a more regional competition, which was a Red, Orange and Green Ball circuit. There's also a teams event called Future Stars. So we tried to cater for each of the different levels of the pathway. So someone who's being introduced to competition for the first time, someone who's a little bit more experienced, is looking to branch out. So it was a mix of internal and external experiences that helped provide great opportunities for the kids to play. But I guess the best way to describe it is to go back to where we started from. So I was coaching at a private school here on the Gold Coast and in conversations we

wanted to start something up. So we started a Red and Orange competition back in 2013, and that was between ourselves and one of the other coaches. So it was a real ground-up approach. So we discussed there's a hole, there aren't these playing opportunities, so we looked to see how we could introduce this inter-club experience for our kids in Red and Orange because they were already starting to play a little bit in green, tournament sales were, but we wanted to provide an environment that was safe, friendly and non-threatening. So it was not high stakes either so that their experience was going to be a positive one. From there, the first future stars evolved and then involved a number of clubs on the Gold Coast. We started off with just the four clubs to start with and then it branched out and expanded significantly from there. Then I guess our first meeting was an RA meeting, so a regional assembly meeting here on the Gold Coast and Shane talked eloquently about what the needs of the kids that we were coaching and came up and we had a conversation afterwards. Yeah, and we put together a blueprint for Red and Orange and put the idea forward to a few other coaches and ran a pilot and here we are. The blueprint, initially it was a red and orange stage because, as I said, we had the green in some form of fixture or competition format, but it was a period of time. So from our first conversation, we developed a blueprint about exactly what we wanted and

the keys behind it were significant in that in order to meet the developmental readiness of the players and what they were capable of achieving, we had to identify a number of different things that we were trying to achieve from it. This blueprint, we still have documented and took a lot of effort and the depth and breadth of it was considerable. From there, we were able to get it off the ground fairly quickly and in fact the tournament that you see in this slide is one of the first tournaments at Somerset and the layout will get into a little bit later on. It was pretty special with kids and it's about making the children feel special and safe in that environment and of course we'll talk about the values later on too, which is more of the outcome. So from there, we thought we'd expand on it and try to add a little bit more sort of icing to the cake and that's when we start the first Gold Coast regional talent camps and we operated it conjunctively with a dear friend of ours, Anthony Richardson and Richo jumped on the chance to be involved in the community here on the Gold Coast and what we did is we included parent education, coach education, some talent identification for the talent side of things, but what did it create a real community in the Gold Coast because it was no longer operating in silos, we were one as one unit. Absolutely and it also brought the coaches together, it was to invite all the coaches

to the talent camp to be on court, looking around at all the kids playing and bringing a collaboration together with everybody. Yeah, so I guess from there we moved into competitive opportunities that would be a representative opportunity for representing the Gold Coast in our respect and you might want to talk to the Bolton Brisbane. Oh look, I think it was great the first couple of years to have the circuit working and I thought it's unfortunate that they didn't have an outcome whereby we could represent our region and play against other regions so we created the Bolton Brisbane which was originally three regions and we had that at the end of the year as our final and you played for your region, Gold Coast against Sunshine Coast and Brisbane. So as you can see from the timeline this is a fairly drawn out process, it didn't happen overnight and it took a lot of relationship building in between to get people on board and I guess that's the biggest thing that the legacy from our initial construct is that we have great relationships with the coaches on the Gold Coast. So looking at the Colourball circuit, so this is the tier that we introduced for the higher competencies. And sitting down we went through so many things, a number that are up on the screen, what age groups and so we might talk to a few of these. So Red we decided that 8 and under would be an appropriate age and the idea being that

the competencies were looking at overarm, so first and second serve. Orange we decided to go 10 and under for the fact that the child could almost create their own pathway by staying in Orange longer instead of coming into Green too early maybe with not the right competencies and Green we decided after a year of changing to 11 and under which was highly successful. So it was interesting as well in terms of the competencies we have on the form that a coach has to sign you off, has to tick you off that you are Red 3 competent so you must adhere to all those competencies because we don't want to provide someone with a terrible experience when they don't have the same level of play as other players in the group where they are going to be beaten significantly each time they step onto the court. So we wanted to create an environment where there was more representative play of what they were going to experience so they were going to feel like they were in every single match and hence those coach signing off on those competencies was a crucial part of it. We adapted the scoring format. Yep so the scoring format for Red was 1-15 so first to 15-14 wins the next point wins and then Orange we went fast for very simple four matches we'll go through the format a bit later on and Green we decided six games so it really leads up to 12 and unders which was effectively more than one set. Yeah so the key was that we didn't want to overload the families too much we wouldn't

put this on the time where the families could come and they would experience it and still have time over the weekend for themselves so it was keeping the player and the family at the forefront of our concerns. When it came to the court sizes and layouts the key was that we would adhere to the tennis australian court sizes and so we stuck with the 10.97 by 8.23 sorry by 5.5 meter court which it is now with the new nets and we stuck with the 18.29 for Orange and 23.77 for the Green size so we tried to keep it in alignment so that their experiences no matter where they played would be just the same. I think for the red ball particularly I think a big win there was having two courts on one court not having four courts laid up next to each other so we created a lot of runoff space. And that also enabled a lot of the smaller clubs to take part in it and that was part of our guiding principles and that we wanted more people involved in it and more clubs involved so by doubling up on the court space effectively you can play a red tournament at a four court six court venue so we were able to bring them into the fold just by manipulating or identifying the size of the courts and the number of courts that would be required which also allows the operators to be educated in tournament directing and working off tournament planner. That's right and they're all implemented in each of the tournaments across the board.

We were pretty clear as well for this level as well we wanted the events separated between the boys and the girls so they had their own event and in match play in-house we created more of a girls versus boys so that's a more supported program outside our venue we were happy to have a gender difference and also for the future stars being a team event it was everyone together so it takes a lot of the focus off my ability to play because I'm part of a team and that was a big part of it. Do you want to talk to the values? Yeah values is a huge part of it and you often wonder why we put young children in competition you know eight and under a lot of people would say that it's probably a bit early but in my opinion if you put the values with it and reward those values we're giving the children an environment of playing competitive tennis you could say but also we're actually highlighting the values of how to behave and what's best for them and on the day we have rewards that are greater than winning the event and those rewards are based on best effort and best sportsmanship. That's an interesting concept because we're putting the person we're looking at this holistic development of the child and the key function of that is we want better people playing our game and we know that if we instill these values in place that we're going to have better people at the end of it who more like where to stay in our sport and this coming year so for 2025

on the Gold Coast circuit there'll be prizes for the four semi-finalists so no longer playing off first, second or third so we're identifying you as great players but the biggest prizes are going to be for the sportsmanship and effort so I think that sends a clear message and also to do with social media as well the social media will be publicizing the big photos of the sportsmanship and effort winners. So you know the financial aspects I think we started out in the IRA with the TIP funding that we have up here of $1,800 to get NETs and so forth and that first year it bought $9,000 in for the region so we actually made money on creating some TIP funding and now I know that that 30 odd tournaments 10 each each color makes up to $45,000 for the region. Yeah it's an incredible investment that the region made in this unique piece of competition space that it has been rewarded and it's value added to the tennis community here on the Gold Coast. One of the big parts of it that differentiates from regular tournament players having a supervisor or a number on court. Yeah look I think from an early stage you know it's pretty hard to concentrate and keep school with those children and if we can have a supervisor standing next to another child that's maybe scoring on a score sheet well there's an educational piece there already and I think every child at play tennis should know how to write a score down and keep score so

we're very big on that supervisor for red and orange green we tend to let them run their own matches and we have a supervisor roaming the center. You know the etiquette is often lost in the competition space but we think it's an integral part about identifying who the person is and that feeling of self and importance all those things that go along with it the way they feel about themselves it's important to have that link between that and tennis and so I think this is where our circuit differences differentiates itself from a lot of other things in that we're providing that opportunity for the kids to be an umpire and experience what that's like with the supervision from older players. Yeah absolutely and then that takes us sort of the parent player education the parent particularly is a it's a child-free friendly zone and so no parents are on the court but by having those supervisors and umpires in place there's no reason for those parents to be on court. That's right they can sit back and be the the spectators that uh and do that we want them to be that's exactly right be supportive of their children and make sure that they have a good time. I think part of that parent education piece too which I think Jay you presented on early on was not just about you know the behavior of the parent on the court but it's about the pathway um I think we had an hour with the parents at one stage we took

them off off the courts and into a room and and and really just worked out you know why we're playing red and orange and green for the period of time that we do. That's right and understanding the components of what the pathway looked like for the hot shots programs going from blue red orange and green to the yellow ball so understanding what the stages were about and what we're trying to teach within each stage. Yeah uh once again that uh the etiquette was we covered basically in the parent education the player education because players uh have a player information session prior to the start of play uh where the what's the expectations are going to be uh designated before the start of play so I think that's a big part of it uh so that they understand what the they have to do and particularly for a red competition when it's new to so many of them uh it's their first playing experience outside the club and then to be thrown into this space we want to make it comforting and also provide them with an understanding of what they need to be doing on the court when they need to be able to check in not to be too far away from the tournament desk at times so understand what the next matches will be etc so and then basically in these spaces we're preparing them for you know 11 12 and under tournaments that's right you know and then we get to the the draw types we make sure that uh each child has four to five

matches a day which we run a compass draw um and in some cases in the red we do some round robins with compass draws um the scheduling is usually eight o'clock starts uh finishing around about 12 30 one o'clock so that the parents can still get a lunch on a Sunday yeah um and keeping it a very family environment um also just enjoying the Sundays with the family but just having a taste of what tournament play could look like that's a big part of it isn't it in each of the ones it will expand for each difference in the section the reds will be a bit shorter than the orange which would be shorter than the greens uh costs uh costs are around $35 to play um and like i said it's uh it's four matches um which gives them you know sort of uh up to an hour and a half play with a bit of rest in between and that price factors work pretty good on the Gold Coast yeah uh administration wise uh because it's run through tp uh tournament entries etc and the scheduling is all done uh it's an opportunity for the club owners or club operators to be able to upskill themselves in uh the administration side of things and the tournament planner and be tournament director so uh in terms of the development of the people within the club land it's a great opportunity if they don't have those skills yeah that's right yeah uh promotional yeah look i think it's been incredible actually the last couple of years tq have taken on board the promotional side

of things and uh and they've done a great job digitally um we now have 10 tournaments in each color which is promoted throughout the Gold Coast also it's has its own website so people can go on on board on colored ball um Gold Coast and see how it all works and find out all the information they need yeah um i think uh the the main thing here is that we get the the word out that that it's there and now we're getting a lot of players from brism coming in that's right um and we want to grow this out so that um we can build a bigger regional sort of series which will lead to a better bulk of brism of course and also lead to more players in our game for longer yeah well that's what it's all about isn't it it's a match play piece that creates that yeah so looking at the breakdown uh this is just a brief run through of where we are in terms of the basics of the format so red bull uh all trying to run within the space of three hours which is great gives the parents an opportunity to to watch their children play number of matches we try to keep consistent across the board at four uh and ensure that the they're always supervised so that they're learning a few different skills outside hitting a tennis ball yeah i think really important though there's the layout you know the layout of the red ball is those two courts on one court and the orange ball is our orange two court but it's also line courts with children so it's a it's a strong line it's not

just markets right now in the court that's right and suddenly they don't move uh and there are no discrepancies in terms of oh that might have been in might have been out uh it's clearly defined this play area because once they identify that it's my court and someone's gone to a lot of effort to make it look like this uh it raises not only the level of play but uh the investment of the child back into the sport which is a huge part of it and i think also by having this as a match play benchmark the coaching program becomes better underneath absolutely absolutely because the competition is the driver of our sport and there are no two ways about it uh as that data suggested earlier on uh would purvey that uh if they don't experience competition well they're not really a tennis player are they they're just having a hit that's right so why don't we train during the week and play on the weekends like most sports do that's right yeah so moving on to future stars so this concept came about uh we wanted to provide an opportunity without being threatening uh lower sort of slightly lower competencies so it was more an introductory opportunity for kids to play outside their own clubs and as i said it started off between two clubs over a day and it expanded incredibly out to over a hundred competitors over 12 clubs and it got so big that we had to separate into north and south divisions because of it uh it was

just getting too big for what we had so in terms of growth what a great opportunity um you might want to talk to the competencies around it oh look we decided that it would be better to have two under arms and um keep it pretty simple delivery is anywhere on a three meter court for red um orange we played only doubles um and now we've just introduced the orange one court as a single score so now it's expanded with the orange and green we we only played doubles as well but we expanded to um singles as well but the idea is that on an orange you can over arm serve a template first serve an under arm on each second so it builds out a larger amount of players to enjoy the game the game of tennis at a competitive level and develops their competence and confidence in in playing the sport uh also that connection with uh there are the teammates and they introduce themselves to to new opponents that they won't have seen before and uh that takes a lot of the scary factor away from it moving forward if they too decide to go into the competitive space but if they stay in this space and play socially it's a great avenue for that as well so the way it worked was we we had eight players per team in red four in orange and four in green and we would come together on one day as six tennis centers and do a north match and a south match on that same day and you'd play four or five of those per year so it was built around one term but the whole entire

coaching program you have a match play program yeah look i think um in the beginning when i first got here i was doing what i thought i knew best which was to coach children and activities and and wondered why we didn't have any um competitive play for eight to nine year olds in red and orange and those eight and nine year olds are playing green ball and not playing it very well so we decided look let's get a red firstly an orange then a red internal match by Friday night competition it turned into four red ball players at the start which was extremely fearful of yeah um but by putting the values to it and and having a lot of support behind it it had built out to 16 players in red and i think 28 in orange which then you know created a platform for this regional play and team play and and also it gave my coaches some some realistic view on what they're working for that's exactly right you know so it's about um building a players competencies to be able to perform in in an outcome of playing a match and the coaches would be all employed on the night and and they'd see their own child that they were coaching during the week play the match that is actually a little bit different than actually doing the activity yeah because we don't actually know how they play if you're not going to watch them so this is a great opportunity or the first stepping stone and actually seeing your child play uh so that then you can work on their development

well it's the difference between live ball and non-live ball that's right you know so when they're playing a live ball it's very different to having a tennis lesson that's not live yeah and the pressure of a match as well yeah so and and we again we put those values heavily around um each each player so that they feel like they're achieving the right things how do you find uh the interactions between the kids do you think it develops that sense of community and a culture within the club so the format that we we um put together was uh one singles match and then two doubles matches even in the red space and the the players that would play against each other in singles would be doubles partners and play against the rest of the group so there was actually a buddy up system and then if there was eight in a group it actually became like a buddy up buddy up system which yeah for me created a very tribal environment and then it felt very safe to actually send those children out to the external match play because they were all supporting each other so ideally we were a football club but we're a tennis club of players and we created that through that system yeah it's a change in the thinking of this being an individual sport this is a club sport or a team sport and once you start to see that evolve that's when the biggest changes will take place for your clubs once again the parent education and player education this is the starting point for
